title: Job, a good man (Job 1–2)
hook: a good man loses everything, and still does not curse God
carry: the lord gave, the lord took

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five books of the Psalms. Your line was every feeling has a psalm. Which one did you choose for this week? Today we leave the Psalms for the hardest book of wisdom. Day four hundred forty-two.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a folk tale, once upon a time, far away. Nobody knows for sure where Uz was. The book never says Job was an Israelite. He's just a man, somewhere east, with seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a habit of getting up early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned at their parties. Then, in a single day, four messengers arrive, one on the heels of the next. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell on the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last one: a great wind hit the house where his children were eating, and they are all dead.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `FOUR MESSENGERS, ONE DAY.` → `EVERYTHING GONE.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible describes Job as "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Perfect here means whole, blameless, not flawless. Before the disasters, the reader is shown something Job never sees: a scene in heaven. The heavenly beings come before God, and among them is one called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The satan, with the word the in front, more like a job title than a name: the adversary, the accuser. Christian tradition has identified him with the devil; some scholars read him here as a member of the heavenly court whose role is to accuse. God points out Job, and the accuser asks the question the whole book turns on: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Is anyone good for free, or only for the reward? Take it all away, and see. So it is taken. And Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then his own body is struck with sores, and he sits in ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. His wife, who has also just lost ten children, says: curse God, and die. And Job answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" Here's what matters for the days ahead. The reader knows about the heavenly scene. Job never finds out. He has to live through all of it without the explanation.
screen: `PERFECT: WHOLE, BLAMELESS` · `HA-SATAN: THE ACCUSER` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `JOB NEVER SEES THE REASON` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone suffering undeservedly. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind someone whose trouble makes no sense. A child who is sick. A friend whose life fell apart through no fault of their own. People in the news who lost everything in a single day. Don't try to explain it. Job's story begins by refusing to. Just hold them steadily in mind. If you pray, you can name them before God and leave the why unanswered. If you don't, wish them strength, and let your attention rest on them, like a hand on a shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Job. A good man from the land of Uz who loses everything, and whose book asks whether anyone loves God for nothing.
Your line: the Lord gave, the Lord took. Today, notice one thing you hold that you didn't earn and can't keep forever, and handle it gently. Day four hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Christians often read the book of Job in times of grief and suffering, and Job's words "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" are said at many Christian funerals.

fork.setup: in one day you've lost your herds, your servants and all ten of your children. what do you do?
options: tear your robe, fall to the ground, and worship.
demand that God explain himself, right now.
fork.reveal: Job grieves with his whole body and still blesses God's name. the demands for an answer come later, and the book keeps those too.

original.note: Hebrew: the adversary, the accuser. in Job it carries the word the, like a title.

trapdoor: what you thought: Job's suffering must be punishment for something he did.
what it means: a good man loses everything, grieves, and still blesses God, without ever learning why.
what a scholar hears: ha-satan with the article, the accuser in the heavenly court, asking whether anyone fears God for nothing.

notes: Index carry 'the lord gave, the lord took' kept exactly (lowercase); spoken as 'the Lord gave, the Lord took'.
'Perfect' (Hebrew tam) glossed as whole, blameless. Confirm.
Ha-satan: script says Christians have long identified him with the devil, and many scholars read him as a member of the heavenly court in the accuser's role. Confirm this is fair to both readings.
Job's wife: 'curse God, and die' (2:9) paraphrased without quotation marks; the script notes she has also lost ten children, to avoid casting her as a villain.
Location of Uz is debated (Edom and the Hauran are both proposed); softened to 'nobody knows for sure'.
Job 1:21 is widely used in Christian funeral rites (e.g. BCP 1662 Burial of the Dead opening sentences). Confirm for howItsDone.
